[AmericanJournalofScience,Vol.310,November,2010,P.1168–1186,DOI10.2475/09.2010.15]
PALEOMAGNETISM OF 1780–1770 MA MAFIC AND COMPOSITE
INTRUSIONS OF SMÅLAND (SWEDEN): IMPLICATIONS FOR THE
MESOPROTEROZOIC SUPERCONTINENT
S.A.PISAREVSKY*,**andG.BYLUND***
ABSTRACT. We present a paleomagnetic study of 1785 to 1770 Ma composite and
maficintrusionsinSmåland,Sweden.Apositiveinversebakedcontacttestsuggeststhe
primary nature of their magnetization. The palaeomagnetic pole (45.7°N, 182.7°E,
(cid:2)
A 8.0°)mayberegardedasakeypoleforFennoscandia.
95
Available paleomagnetic data suggest that Laurentia and Fennoscandia/Baltica
driftedtogethersince1780Mauntilatleast1265Ma.Thesetwocontinentscouldform
acoreofahypotheticalMesoproterozoicsupercontinent.
Key words: Paleoproterozoic, Fennoscandia, Trans-scandinavian Igneous Belt,
Sarmatia,paleomagnetism,Smålandporphyries,Nunasupercontinent
introduction
The hypothesis of Precambrian supercontinents has been strongly debated in
recent decades (for example, Piper, 1976, 2000; Rogers, 1996; Condie, 2000; Meert,
2002; Pesonen and others, 2003; Zhao and others, 2004). The recent UNESCO IGCP
440project“RodiniaAssemblyandBreakup”(Bogdanovaandothers,2008a)markeda
significantbreakthroughinourunderstandingoftheyoungestPrecambriansupercon-
tinent, Rodinia. However, its exact configuration and history is still controversial (for
example,Dalziel,1997;Pisarevskyandothers,2003;Liandothers,2008,2009),owing
mainlytothesmallnumberofNeoproterozoichigh-quality,well-datedpaleomagnetic
polesavailable.ThesituationforMesoproterozoicandoldertimesisevenworse.Evans
andPisarevsky(2008)estimatedthenumberofhigh-qualitypre-800Mapaleomagnetic
poles(paleopoles)atlessthanfifty.ThisisnotenoughtoconstructadequateApparent
PolarWanderPaths(APWPs)—themajortoolforPhanerozoicreconstructions.Hence
itisnecessarytorelyprimarilyonthe“keypole”approach(Buchanandothers,2000),
which causes additional problems such as polarity ambiguity and longitudinal uncer-
tainty. Although those problems can be partly resolved by comparison of coeval
paleopoles from different continents(Cawood and others,2006;EvansandPisarevsky
2008),thereareveryfewcoevalpairsofpaleopolesavailable.
Traces of the widespread Late Paleoproterozoic orogenic events in various conti-
nentspersuadesomeworkerstosuggesttheexistenceoftheMesoproterozoicsupercon-
tinent called Nuna by Hoffman (1997), but also known as Columbia or Hudsonland
(for example, Condie, 2000; Rogers and Santosh, 2002; Meert, 2002; Pesonen and
others,2003;Zhaoandothers,2004).Meert(2002)analyzedsomenon-keypaleopoles
and proposed that this supercontinent was assembled after ca. 1770 Ma. Some recent
paleomagnetic data, however, suggest that some building blocks of Nuna (Laurentia
and Baltica) were fixed with respect to each other from ca. 1750 Ma until ca. 1270 Ma
(Irving and others, 2004; Salminen and Pesonen, 2007). These results imply a
long-lived connection between Laurentia and Baltica with north-eastern (present
coordinates) Baltica facing south-eastern Greenland (for example, Patchett and
Bylund, 1977; Stearn and Piper, 1984; Park, 1992; Starmer, 1996). The proposed

connectionissupportedbygeologicalsimilaritiesbetweenArcheancrustalblocksand
Proterozoic orogenic belts in two continents (for example, Winchester, 1988; Gower
andothers,1990;GorbatschevandBogdanova,1993).However,additionalpaleomag-
netictestsarerequiredtoverifythisconnection.
Post-Svecofennian (ca. 1800-1750 Ma) rocks of Fennoscandia have undergone
extensive paleomagnetic study (see Pisarevsky and Sokolov, 2001 for an overview).
Despite the consistency of the paleopoles, most of them are not supported by robust
evidencefortheprimaryremanenceandonlyafewarepreciselydated.Consequently,
1870to1750MaFennoscandianpoleswereusuallynotcitedas“reliable”(forexample,
Evans and Pisarevsky, 2008), or as “key poles” (Buchan and others, 2000) used in
paleogeographicapplications.
Nilsson and Wikman (1997) dated two composite intrusions in Småland, Sweden
(cid:2) (cid:3) (cid:4)
(figs. 1A and 1B) at 1780 3 and 1776 8/ 7 Ma (U-Pb zircon) correspondingly.
Nilsson(1992)demonstratedthatmaficmagmatisminSmålandisprobablygenetically
related (and so coeval) to these composite intrusions. Here we present results of a
paleomagnetic study of these and some composite mafic-felsic and mafic intrusions in
theSmålandarea.
geology and sampling
The studied area (fig. 1) belongs to the 1.81 to 1.76 Ga Småland-Va¨rmland
belt—the southern and oldest part of the Trans-scandinavian Igneous Belt (TIB)
formed mainly by reworking of the juvenile 2.10 to 1.87 Ga Svecofennian crust in a
continental-arc setting (Ho¨gdahl and others, 2004). In the west, the TIB is bound by
the Eastern Segment of the 1.14 to 0.95 Ga Sveconorwegian orogen along the
Sveconorwegian Frontal Deformational Zone, or Protogine Zone (for example, Gor-
batschevandBogdanova,1993,2004).
Mafic and felsic plutons and dikes are widespread in the Småland-Va¨rmland belt.
IntheeasternpartsoftheSmålandprovinceaspecialsetofcompositedikeshasbeen
found. These dikes are mainly composed of a marginal mafic and a central felsic part.
To varying degree magma mixing features between the two parts can be observed. In
the literature they are described under the general name of “Småland dyke porphy-
ries”. Some of these dike porphyries do not have mafic margins (Nilsson, 1992).
Composite dikes are often regarded as a final product in a complex evolution with
interplay between coeval felsic and mafic magmas (for example, Frost and Mahood,
1987). The specific structure of the Småland porphyries with the mafic material
generally along the dike walls, has been interpreted with a special type of intrusion
mechanism(forexample,Carriganandothers,1992;Eichelberger,1995)inwhichthe
maficmagmaduetoitslowviscosity,hasfacilitatedthetransportofthefelsicmagmain
the same way as water is used as lubricant along the walls in an oil pipe line. These
relationships suggest that the mafic components have the same age as the radiometri-
callydatedfelsicparts.
Radiometric dating (U-Pb, zircons) of the felsic component in the composite
dikeshasbeenreportedbyNilssonandWikman(1997).SamplesfromthePåskallavik
(cid:2)
and Alsterbro intrusions have been analyzed, resulting in 1780 3 Ma for the former
(cid:3) (cid:4)
and 1776 8/ 7 Ma for the latter. These ages are somewhat, but not significantly
younger than the ambient granitoids confirming the conclusions (for example,
Persson, 1985) that the dike porphyries are the final expression of the granite
magmatisminthearea.
A major, mainly geochemical, investigation of these and other related dikes has
beenmadebeNilsson(1992).Oneofhisresultsisthatthemaficpartsinthecomposite
dikeshaveasimilarchemistryassomemaficdikeswithoutafelsiccomponent,butwith
the same NW-trending direction in the northwestern part and mainly ENE-trending
directionfortherestoftheinvestigatedarea.Thisdikeswarm,calledthe“Oskarshamn

dykes”,isthereforeinferredtobethesameageasthecompositedikes.Ayoungerdike
swarm, the “Vimmerby dykes” with a general NE-trending direction is geochemically
different.Fieldobservationsconfirmingthisrelativeagedifferencehasalsobeenmade
by Persson (1985), however the absolute age of the Vimmerby dykes is unclear. A few
larger mafic intrusions also outcrop in the area. Our paleomagnetic data suggest that
theyarelikelytoberelatedtotheOskarshamndykes.
Some mafic dikes of the 978 to 946 Ma Blekinge-Dalarna swarm (So¨derlund and
others,2005)werefoundintheeasternpartoftheareaandstudiedpaleomagnetically
(Bylund,1985,1992;PisarevskyandBylund,1998).
In Alsterbro and Påskallavik (fig. 1B) we collected oriented block samples for the
paleomagnetic study of both the composite intrusions dated by Nilsson and Wikman
(1997). Additionally we sampled two more composite dikes (Ignatorp and Bo¨ta
Kvarn), four mafic dikes (Emmaboda, Oskarhamn, and Alsterbro), and two large
gabbroic bodies (Stenberga and Virserum). Sample locations are shown in figure 1B.
Studied composite dikes are ca. 10 to 70 m thick, mafic dikes are 0.5 to 3 m thick.
Nilsson(1992)reportedthatthefelsiccoresofthecompositedikesaremoreresistant
to alteration than the mafic edges, so we concentrated our efforts on the fine-grained
groundmassofthesefelsiccores.Atotalof150orientedblockswerecollectedfrom20
sites. Both magnetic and sun compasses were used for the orientation. Sampled
localitiesareshowninfigure1B,andthecoordinatesareintable1.
analytical techniques
In the laboratory from 2 to 12 cylindrical specimens (25 mm diameter) were
drilledfromeachorientedblock.Duringsamplinganddrillingofporphyrieswetried
to avoid large phenocrysts, so all our specimens are from the relatively fine-grained
matrix.
Samples were analyzed in the paleomagnetic laboratory of Lund University
(Sweden) and in the Tectonics Special Research Centre at the University of Western
Australia.Magneticremanencewasmeasuredusing2Gcryogenicmagnetometersand
a JR-5 spinner magnetometer (Geofyzika, Brno, Czech Republic.) Stepwise thermal
demagnetizations,upto600to650°C,andprogressivealternatingfield(AF)demagne-
tizations, up to 160 mT, were applied using Schonstedt TSD-1, Magnetic Measure-
ments TD2 furnaces, and a 2G600 automated degaussing system. Normally 3 or 4
cylinders (in some cases up to eight) from each oriented block were demagnetized.
The mean characteristic remanence (ChRM) directions for each oriented block were
calculated and used for the site mean calculations (table 1). Magnetic mineralogy was
investigated from demagnetization characteristics, saturation isothermal remanent
magnetization (SIRM) curves and, in selected samples, from detailed variation of
susceptibilityversustemperature(20to700°C)obtainedusingtheBartingtonmeterin
conjunctionwithanautomatedBartingtonfurnace.SIRMcharacteristicswerestudied
by inducing fields with a Molspin Ltd magnetic pulse charger for fields up to 200 mT
andaRedcliffe700BSMpulsechargerforfieldsupto4T.

After removal of a low-stability viscous overprint, both thermal and AF demagnetiza-
tion isolated a single stable ChRM in three intrusions (Alsterbro, Ignatorp, Bo¨ta
Kvarn). This ChRM has shallow downward (very shallow upward in a few samples)
N-NNE direction (figs. 4A and 4B; table 1, entries 1-9). Demagnetization behavior of
porphyries from the Påskallavik intrusion is similar to three other intrusions, but the
directionsareveryscattered,soweexcludedthisbodyfromoverallmeanscalculations
andwedonotshowthesedataintable1.
DoleriteDike(Emmaboda)
The intensity of NRM of the dolerites ranges from 10 to 1000 mA/m, and their
magnetic susceptibility is around 0.5 to 1.0
(cid:5)

(cid:7)

SD-PSDmagnetite.Thisinferenceissupportedby“squareshoulder”thermaldemagne-
tization curves (fig. 4C). Apart from viscous remanence, only one magnetite-bearing
NRM component with N-NNW medium to shallow downward direction was isolated
(fig.4C;table1,entry10).AllstudiedsamplesyieldcoherentChRM.

The intensity of NRM of the Stenberga gabbro varies from 100 to 9000 mA/m,

(cid:7)

andMcElhinny(1990)isindeterminate.

AlsterbroMinorDikes,InverseContactTest
ThermalandAFdemagnetizationsofthesampledcountrygranitesdidnotisolate
anystableChRM,sothedirectcontacttestwasimpossible.
However, stable ChRMs were found in two thin mafic dikes intruded into the
Alsterbro composite intrusion. In addition, exocontacts of these thin dikes were
completelyremagnetizedduringtheiremplacement.Themagneticpropertiesofthese
dikesaresimilartootherdoleritesinthisstudyandoneChRMcomponentwasisolated
in each dike. The ChRM directions differ from each other and from the mean
direction of the main intrusion (figs. 7A, 7C, and 7E; table 1, entries 13, 15). Dike 3
(fig. 7A) is apparently “reversely” (upward) magnetized and its mean remanence
direction resembles the “Sveconorwegian” direction of the 978 to 946 Ma Blekinge–
Dalarna dikes (for example Bylund, 1985, 1992; Pisarevsky and Bylund, 1998; Bylund
(cid:6)
and Pisarevsky, 2002). In particular, the remanence direction of dike 3 (D 297°;
(cid:6)(cid:4)
I 48°) is very close to the remanence direction of nearby Åseda dolerites and they
(cid:6) (cid:6)(cid:4)
have the same polarity (D 304°; I 38°; Pisarevsky and Bylund, 1998). The rema-
nenceofdike2ismorescattered,hasanoppositepolaritywithrespecttotheChRMof

discussion
ChRM directions of three out of four studied composite intrusions are coherent
and supported by the baked contact test. This direction corresponds to the time of
theiremplacementat1785to1770Ma.ThePåskallavikcompositeintrusionrevealeda
highlyscatteredChRMandwasexcludedfromthefurtheranalyses.Boththermaland
AF demagnetizations of dolerite and gabbro (sites 14 and 15) isolated stable ChRMs
with opposite polarities and with similar (but not identical) directions to those of the

composite intrusions. This similarity suggests that the Emmaboda dike belongs to the
Oskarhamnswarm(Nilsson,1992)andconfirmstheabovementionedsuggestionthat
mafic dikes of this swarm and Småland gabbroic intrusions are only slightly younger
than the composite intrusions. Taking this into account we calculated the mean
paleopoleforthestudiedSmålandcompositeandmaficintrusions(table1),whichwe
considertoprovidetheca.1780MakeypoleforFennoscandia.
On the other hand, the dolerite dike near Oskarhamn and minor dike 2 in
Alsterbro, whose primary remanence is supported by the baked contact test, are
significantly younger. These dikes are not dated, but the calculated paleopoles (table
1,entries12and13)areclosetothemean1460MapaleopoleforBaltica(table2,entry
4). However, these paleopoles should be treated cautiously because of their rather
uncertainageconstraints.Theprimary(supportedbythecontacttest)ChRMofminor
dike 3 in Alsterbro is similar to the remanence directions of the 978 to 946 Ma
Blekinge-Dalarna mafic dikes (So¨derlund and others, 2005), and in particular to the
(cid:8)
remanencedirectionoftheÅsedadike(PisarevskyandBylund,1998)locatedjust 30
km NW of Alsterbro. Hence we tentatively assume the 978 to 946 Ma age for the
Alsterbrodoleritedike3.
Buchanandothers(2000)didnotfindasinglekeypolefromFennoscandiaolder
(cid:8)
than 1640 Ma. Pisarevsky and Sokolov (2001) reported a study of the Shoksha
Formation redbeds supported by a conglomerate test and by the presence of the
magnetostratigraphypattern(SHpoleintable2,entry2).Pesonenandothers(2003)
(cid:2)
consideredthispoleasakeypole.TheShokshaFormationpredatesthe1770 12Ma
(cid:8)
Ropruchey sill (Bibikova and others, 1990) and postdates the 1800 Ma underlying
PetrozavodskFormation(Sokolovandothers,1987).Howeverthelatterdate(K-Aron
glauconite) is not considered as very reliable, so the exact age of this pole is unclear.
Our new ca.1780 Ma pole from the Småland intrusions has better age constraints and
is supported by the inverse contact test (SM pole in table 2, entry 1). The angular
difference between SH and SM poles is 28° and probably reflects their age difference.
The similarity to the combined paleopole of the 1770 Ma Ropruchey Sill in
Karelia,Russia(Dammandothers,1997;Fedotovaandothers,1999)(RPpoleintable
2, entry 3) suggests that the age of the SH pole is closer to the younger limit of the
original1790to1770MaestimationbyPisarevskyandSokolov(2001).
Reliable Late Paleoproterozoic and Mesoproterozoic paleopoles are scanty and
notsufficientforunequivocalpaleogeographicreconstructions.Table2clearlydemon-
stratesthisforLaurentiaandBaltica,andthesituationformostoftheothercontinents
is worse (for example, Evans and Pisarevsky, 2008). However, these poles can be used
for testing some reconstructions based on geological data. We shall follow this
approachhere.
Salminen and Pesonen (2007) obtained a new robust 1460 Ma paleopole for
BalticaandproposedanewreconstructionofLaurentiaandBalticaintheMesoprotero-
zoic between 1460 and 1270 Ma. Moreover, following the suggestion of Pesonen and
others(2003),SalminenandPesonen(2007)usednewpaleomagneticdatafrom1740
MaCleaverDykes(Irvingandothers,2004)andtheabovementionedSHBalticanpole
toproposethatLaurentiaandBalticacouldhavebeenconnectedby1790to1770Ma.
Interestingly,theLaurentia-BalticareconstructionofSalminenandPesonen(2007)is
similar, but not identical to the reconstruction of Gower and others (1990) built by
matching pre-Neoproterozoic crustal blocks and orogenic belts of these cratons. The
difference between the “geological” reconstruction of Gower and others (1990) and
“paleomagnetic” reconstruction of Salminen and Pesonen (2007) is minimal and we
think that they are within the precision limits of paleomagnetic and geochronological
methods.

### page_14
intrusionsofSmåland(Sweden):implicationsforthemesoproterozoicsupercontinent 1181
Unfortunately Gower and others (1990) did not provide Euler rotation parame-
tersfortheirreconstruction.Wetriedtoreproducetheirreconstructiontothebestof
ourabilitiesanddeducedthefollowingEulerrotationparameters:Balticawasrotated
withrespecttoLaurentiaat45°anticlockwisearoundtheEulerpoleof45°N,7.5°E.We
applied this Euler pole for the paleogeographic reconstructions shown in figure 8
(table 3). Clearly these reconstructions fit paleomagnetic data (table 2) reasonably
well. There are some minor differences between our selection of paleopoles (table 2)
andthechoiceofSalminenandPesonen(2007).First,insteadofthe1740MaCleaver
Dykes pole (Irving and others, 2004), we used the mean 1760 to 1740 Ma Laurentian
pole calculated by the same authors. Second, we excluded the Spokane Formation
pole(VitorelloandVanderVoo,1977)fromthe1460MameanLaurentianpole.This
pole was subsequently considered to represent a burial remagnetization (Elston and
others,2002).
A comparison of the 1770 to 1740 Ma paleomagnetic data from Ukraine (Elming
and others, 2001) with non-key Fennoscandian poles suggests that Baltica was not yet
assembled at that time. This interpretation places some constraints on the timing of
the collision between Sarmatia-Volgouralia and Fennoscandia (Bogdanova, 1993;
Gorbatschev and Bogdanova, 1993; Bogdanova and others, 2008b) and we included
our interpretation of this event in the reconstructions (fig. 8). A similar model has
beenrecentlypublishedbyElmingandothers(2010).
Table 2 shows that there are two roughly coeval pairs of Laurentian and Baltican
paleopolesat1460and1265Ma,butthesituationismorecomplicatedforthe1780to
1750Matimeinterval.AgemismatchesbetweenLaurentianandFennoscandianpoles
exceed ten million years, so we cannot use their exact matching for the reconstruc-
tions. Instead we made a general assumption that Laurentia and Fennoscandia were
parts of a single continent and their mutual configuration did not change for the
whole time interval considered. The above mentioned estimated Euler rotation
parameters were used to reconstruct this configuration. Then we reconstructed this
joint continent (which could be part of some larger continent) paleomagnetically for
three time slices using 1780 Ma (SM pole), 1770 Ma (RP and SH poles), and 1750 Ma
(LA1750pole).ThesethreereconstructionsshowreasonablysmoothdriftofLaurentia-
Fennoscandiaanddemonstratethattheirfitispaleomagneticallypermissive.Asimpli-
fied (after Li and others, 2008) geological legend is also shown in those reconstruc-
tions. The chain of 1.8 to 1.6 Ga orogens (shown in black) suggests that the joint
continent had a long-lived western active margin, as was proposed previously (for
example,Karlstromandothers,2001).
The Sarmatian KO paleopole is shown in the 1750 Ma reconstruction and
demonstrates that the final collision between Fennoscandia and Sarmatia-Volgouralia
was not completed at that time. The final docking probably occurred at ca. 1700 Ma
(Bogdanovaandothers,2008b;Elmingandothers,2010),formingBaltica.
Paleomagneticreconstructionsat1460and1265Ma(fig.8)demonstratethatthe
proposed Laurentia-Baltica configuration may have persisted for about 500 m.y. We
suggestthatthesetwocontinentscouldformacoreofahypotheticalMesoproterozoic
supercontinent Nuna (Columbia, Hudsonland). Wingate and others (2009) reported
that Siberia also could have been part of this supercontinent by at least ca. 1500 Ma
according to new high-quality paleomagnetic data. Importantly, their paleomagneti-
cally permissive ca. 1475 Ma reconstruction (see fig. 9 of Wingate and others, 2009)
shows Siberia not in close connection with Laurentia-Baltica. That reconstruction
leaves a space for another continent (or continents) of the size of Laurentia between
Siberia and Laurentia-Baltica, making the hypothetical Nuna comparable to Gond-
wana.ThereforetherecentpaleomagneticdataprovideastrongsupportfortheNuna

conclusions
— ApaleomagneticstudyofSmålandcompositeandmaficintrusionsresultedin
anewrobust1780MapalepoleforFennoscandia.
— This study, in conjunction with other paleopoles from Baltica and Laurentia,
suggest that their mutual position and orientation was unchanged since 1780
Mauntil1265Ma.
— Baltica and Laurentia could form a core of the hypothetical Mesoproterozoic
supercontinentNuna.
